segments.text: Hello everyone.
Mr. CP John perhaps would be the only communist minister in the country today.
So he has a very unique position in India's political landscape.
He is of course Kerala's transport minister, a veteran of Kerala politics for nearly five decades.
He's a lawyer by training and a long time left leader.
So since you have a very unique position as I just said in India's political landscape, so let's begin by asking you, what do you think is leading to the decline of the left?
See, you're right in the sense that I'm the only communist minister in India now.
But it's not a credit to me because there were dozens of ministers in our country from Tripura, West Bengal and Kerala, right from 1967 onwards.
There was no break.
Unfortunately, other communist parties, mainly the mainstream, so-called mainstream communist parties, have declined in their political positions.
And in that sense, I'm a precipitate.
So I'm not boasting about my position.
It's a sad position because there is only one communist minister in the country.
Why do you think that has happened?
You know, once upon a time we have seen left in several states dominate the politics from Tripura to Kerala.
Not only Tripura to Kerala, yeah, Tripura to Kerala, but from your state Bihar,
Left was one of the biggest contingents in politics, even in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Pancha, Maharashtra, even in UP.
In 1967, Varanasi constituency, there was a CPM MP from Varanasi.
So left was a big presence in our country, but unfortunately it declined.
This decline is universal in the sense that across the world, for example, Italian Communist Party declined.
It was one of the biggest communist parties in democracies.
And the Communist Party of Great Britain, it is still the French Communist Party in which Picasso was a member and Spanish Communist Party.
When you look at the European communist movement, it has been declining.
maybe according to our understanding of my party's understanding, maybe due to the dearth of democracy inside the communist parties and as well as in the societies where communist party reigned.
So the young generation who are very much interested in democratic
dealings right from the classroom, right from the home, right from their parents.
They have to have democracy everywhere, every point where they live.
So Communist Party unfortunately forgot
to say that we are really democratic.
And they themselves declared that when we come to power, we will declare the dictatorship of the proletariat.
So my party, it's a small political party, said the dictatorship of the proletariat is not at all a good slogan.
with which you can attract the new generation who are very much bothered about democracy and who are against the dictatorships in any term, any sense of the term.
So, but are there efforts being made by, say, you within your party to connect with a new generation which is speaking a completely different language?
They may not be even ideologically committed.
They just get inspired by certain issues.
It's very also temporary with them.
Yeah.
The temporary political upsurges has become a permanent thing.
So many temporary things come.
See, when you look at Hong Kong, there is a big umbrella march.
And when you look at New York, there was another, isn't it, big movement.
And in many parts of the world, you can see that so many temporary things come and they subside.
So the new generation is not bothered, I think, about a straight jacket ideology per se.
We are living in an old world.
I am old.
I know that I am old.
But you have to propose a democratic ideology, not only in its content, but it in its form, so that youngsters will look at it, I think so.
So let's come to the idea of the new Kerala that the Chief Minister has spoken about.
And you have the task of implementing the entire integrated infrastructure, you know, the roads, the railways, the concern with regards to ports.
He speaks about making Kerala an aviation hub.
you know, it's one thing that the state can do.
For most of it, implementation of this idea, you need the support from the center.
Has that… has that collaboration really happened with the center?
Yes, as far as our government led by Sri V. D. Sathishan is concerned, we are not ready to confront with the union government in governance.
But in politics, we have our own ideologies and our own political positions.
I met Gadgariji within one month to talk to him about so many things around about this mobility thing.
I think he did some good thing in the mobility administration.
And as far as Kerala is concerned, now we are very much bothered about the accident rate.
Nearly 4,000 people die in Kerala.
So right from next week or next month, we are going to launch a high voltage campaign to reduce the fatality from accident death from 4,000 to 2,000, making it 50%.
So it is a big campaign.
It will be a big campaign.
And we have to rally right from the nursery class children
to the old age, the pedestrians, the cyclists, the bus passengers, everyone.
So we are thinking about a new culture in mobility.
As far as my department is concerned, we are very much bothered about the connectivity, the last mile connectivity, and especially the public transport.
As you know, we have introduced a scheme called Priyadarshini in which any woman passenger can travel without any ticket or card or anything in the ordinary basis.
Our ordinary basis constitute sixty-seven percent of our fleet.
Since you spoke about Priyadarshini scheme, there was a comment of yours which went viral.
No, it was a misunderstanding.
I stand for Priyadarshani.
So was it about paraphrasing what really happened with that because you first stood by your acting poor line and then you apologize.
So what really happened then?
No, no, no.
It was an accidental thing.
I always stand for Priyadarshani and the scheme.
Some journalists picked up two, three words, extracted.
That's not a matter of interest now.
So let's move beyond and say that if for every one rupees that the state government is spending on public infrastructure, how much of support are you getting from outside?
I mean, is there private players and have you found takers for your ideas?
Yeah, yeah.
See, for example, I shall tell you, as far as KSRTC is concerned, we are trying to strategize our operations.
by reducing the capex in many ways.
One thing we are requesting our MLAs, there is a government order now, they will be purchasing buses for KSRTC.
MLAs will be purchasing?
Yeah.
And I think I will be getting nearly 300 buses this year, or within one or two years.
And we are requesting the local governments to purchase buses.
and giving to KSRTC in their locality.
We'll operate in their locality.
Even for MLAs, we will be operating this bus in their constituencies, right?
And one thing has happened.

A cooperative society called Calicut City Cooperative Society governed by my colleagues and founded by my friend CN Vijayakrishnan, they gave me 40 lakhs and we bought a bus and we are giving them a bus according to their proposal.
So if you want KSRTC to run in your own constituency or in your village or in an around that… Let them buy the bus and I will operate.
By that I am reducing the capex, meaning capital expenditure.
Right?
And again, we have taken buses for lease, so-called wet leasing.
Now there are few buses in our fleet owned by the private operators and operated by us.
And today, a tender will be opened for the Sabarimala season.
We think around 500 buses we will be getting.
So this has happened in the last three months of your government?
Exactly.
So many things are happening.

Okay, so let's move ahead, you know, because… And moreover, our reservation system has been improved in the sense that you can use the WhatsApp number and using the AI, you can book a ticket in my KSRTC.
And Uber has come to KSRTC.
Through the Uber app, you can book a cab as well as a KSRTC bus.
So you have a collaboration with Uber on this.
Okay, so the extra burden is about 90 crore a month because of the ridership doubling.
If that is the correct data that I have, where does that money actually come from?
Because KSRTC actually doesn't really have much money.
It is not a secret.
See, Priyadarshani scheme is proposed by the government of Kerala.
not by KSRTC.
So fortunately, the finance minister, our chief minister, is kind enough to set apart a good amount in the budgetary proposals.
And we have a budgetary location for the Priyadarshini.
So it is not a burden of KSRTC.
And have the number of buses that your group runs gone down?
And that's why you've increased it and asked more and more MLAs to add to the number of the fleet?
No, no, no, not at all.
We have 5,750 buses.
We have not reduced any bus.
But we want to increase the number of buses in our fleet.
And my wild hope is I have to increase it up to 10,000.
We are ready to take private buses into our fold, if they are willing, for a per kilometer rate.
any kind of PPP or revenue sharing model, nothing.
They can give us their bus, we will take it, we will operate it and we will give per kilometer rate according to the tender.
Logistics is an important area here and that will perhaps define competitiveness among states.
Is there an understanding with the industry bodies that in order to make Kerala a hub, you'll have to live up to what has been done by the neighboring states?
You know, say Hyderabad, what they have achieved in terms of their transport,
a grid and other states including the capital city of Tamil Nadu.
Beyond Vallarapadam at Cochin, we have another big international port at Trivandrum.
It's called Vizhenyam port.
It started happening right from 1992 when my founder leader, M.E.
Ragan, was the port minister.
But finally it happened.
So this Vizhenyam port, international port, is the hub of
the cargo movement.
And connecting the Vizhinjam port, we have the uncompleted NH-66.
It is connected from Vizhinjam, Vallarpadam, Mangalapuram, Goa and Mumbai.
So this NH-66, as well as Vizhinjam and Vallarpadam,
have given us big opportunity for the freight movement.
And the logistics side, even KSRTC is thinking about coming to the area of this cargo movement beyond passenger movement.
So you see that becoming almost a defining moment for the entire economic ecosystem.
Yeah.
Not just a port.
Not just a port.
Our Chief Minister is very clear about it.
He has announced Samudra project type of thing and we have small ports at Calicut, it's called Bepore and Kuala Lumpur, Alleppey.
We have very… it's a series of ports in the western coast.
So connecting all these ports, we can have a good, good
system of maritime movement as well as cargo movement, and it will be a window to the rest of the country, especially in the southern peninsula and the western side.
You know, all this plan, many would say, Mr. John, that it appears good on the paper, but how do you connect these ports?
See, it has been happening.
Virginia is not on the paper.
It has happened.
The biggest ship in the world
is coming to Virinam, it has already come.
But the Samudra project that the Prime Minister… that the Chief Minister of the state has envisaged, how do you implement that?
How do you connect these various ports that you're speaking?
Yeah, we have our, what do you call, vision document ready and we will be implementing it within one or two years.
We have our own clear vision and mission we are confident about.
Okay, so what is it that your government is doing differently from what Pinaray Vijayan did?
See, Pinaray Vijayan, meaning he's not a person.
See, unfortunately, right from 1996, his party, he was not the biggest leader in that party at that time.
1996, he was a minister.
They were not interested in the infrastructure in the PPP mode.
They were against these so-called colleges, unaided colleges.
They were fighting against it.
So their ideological bankruptcy was very clear right from 1991.
They could not cope up with the new economic policies.
after 1991, which China did, which CPM didn't do.
This is one of the main reasons for the decline.

See, everybody is talking about China, but what China is doing, of course there is a dearth of democracy, but it's a surge of development because they are combining capital as well as labor in their country in the cleverest
manner, isn't it?
But in the Indian left as well as other left parties did not understand the Chinese method of governance.
But as far as my party is concerned, my friend is concerned.
We are well aware, right from 1991, that we have to have new methods of democracy, as well as new methods of development.
Now, Pindarai Vijayan's party is talking about PPPs, Virenyampoort.
Now means five years ago or 10 years ago, like Rupan Wingal, they are saying that, yes, yes, it is good.
But they lagged behind.
And the last five years, that government did something in the virinjam port sector.
We are continuing it.
But you just imagine, they declared an inquiry against Umanshanti, the then chief minister.
For what?
For signing the virinjam document.
And later, they implemented the virinjam port with Adani.
They said Umarjandi took a huge amount of 6,000 crores from Adani.
The whole project is less than that.
So that kind of political blunders they were committing.
And the inquiry was nothing.
And the inquiry revealed that nothing happened.
And nothing, the Gowri commissioner, he could not write anything about Umarjandi.
So this is the difference between LDF and UDF.
that UDF is open to investment from whosoever, irrespective of the fact that Rahul Gandhi criticizes Adanis in Delhi.
That is a political thing.
Of course Adani is an industrialist or a company and Rahul Gandhi has his own reservations, Congress party has their own reservations about it.
But when we float the tender,
we have to sign with the person who takes the tender.
Omanjandi did it.
That's it.
So you don't see politics and the development of the state separate or are you of the opinion that they should be placed separately and the interest of the state is primary here?
See of course politics has its own space and we have to oppose those people who are corrupt
At the same time we have to see that something has to be happened in the state like Kerala where we are lagging behind in industrial development.
I was having a conversation with you before you came on the dais and you had said that Kerala has the challenge of demography in terms of how
it's largely the elderly who are now in the state.
That's the challenge that we see from outside as well, that those who are young, they tend to leave the state for better opportunities and growth.
What is it being done by your government to ensure that the young population stays in the state?
See, in that sense, we have become a victim of the success.
success.
Because longevity is a success, isn't it?
We can live beyond 70.
I am reaching 70.
I behave like a person in fifties.
So, you can see so many people beyond seventy, very active in politics, even in sports, even in veteran sports or in business.
Anywhere you look at the community, you can see thousands of people.
It is around twenty percent in some districts like Patananditta.
and is around 15% of the population, is about beyond 60.
Even beyond 70, a good number of people are active.
That is our success.
But our government, what we did, we formed a department for the elderly people.
We called it vayojana vaguppa, meaning department… What the elderly, elderly.
Chieftain is holding that portfolio.
But what is the department for the youth?
Department of youth is the… for many years.
And you asked another question, why people are going outside?
This is not a new phenomena.
Right from 1970, we started in big numbers to the Gulf countries, then to Europe, then to United States, then to Australia, New Zealand, and so many other places across the globe.
One thing I shall tell you, why we are migrating, we are able to migrate.
We are competent enough
to migrate to United States.
We are competent enough to migrate to Paris or Tokyo or London.
This is again our success, number one.
And due to the money value
But Mr. John, don't you think that if the youth or this competent people leave the state, then how will the state really move ahead?
Don't you think the real challenge is to keep your talent pool in the state?
It's a complex question.
See, right from 90s, what happened?
When we were not migrating, was Kerala a good state?
No.
We became prosperous
after our migration.
Remit its economy.
Exactly.
And moreover, from 1991, the value of rupee was devalued, isn't it?
And thousand dollars meant 17,000 rupees.
Now it is one lakh rupees.
Right?
So we are a successful society which could migrate positively to all parts of the country, meaning world.
But now there is another phenomena.
It is not a migration.
It is an exodus.
Exodus is a negative thing.
They are not coming back.
They are not remitting money.
They are not interested in living here.
That is the question.
Migration is not bad, but exodus is bad.
So about that we have to be very careful and moreover we have to provide good education for our youngsters.
Now people are going to the universities.
My daughter studied in United Kingdom.
My younger daughter studied in Vienna, still studying in Vienna.
So well and good, if they are coming back, they are remitting money, that's good.
If they are leaving our state forever, then it is not good.
Are they coming back?
Yes, yeah, they will be coming back I think soon.
This is their decision.
All right, thank you so much for this conversation and thank you for sharing your thoughts.
Okay, thank you.
